It really depends on where you are and what organization you are raising for.

If you do an event one of the quickest ways to bring in extra money is have a "staged donor" announce "impromptu" that they would like to donate so many thousands of dollars. This will spark about ten minutes worth of audience members raising hands and offering to pledge additional donations. These are not fake donors, but usually a high end donor who gives a large sum every year. You put a call into them and request that instead of mailing in their check this year you would like them to "offer it" at the event. It can be formal where they give a speech on why they support and at the end present their check, followed by rounds of them asking "I want to get three people on board right now along with my donation to pledge $1000 (wait for audience to raise hand...make sure you have one $1000 donor planted in audience to get the hand raising started - might be a good idea if this high end don't invites a friend they know will give $1,000 and will raise their hand too), ok now I want five people to give $500 (raise hands) , ten to give $100...on and on until "can everyone else here at least commit to $10 today?" By that time you know you will receive $10 from at least 40% of the audience. if you have 500 people, congrats you just banked $2,000 + all the high end gifts. If played right you can make $10,000 from the ask alone. Not including the price of the event ticket.

It's pretty rare for animals to take care of their elderly. It has been documented that elephants do it. A few socially organized insects such as ants and bees will take care of their mother (i.e. the queen) as it is crucial for the group to survive. In most cases where animals work and hunt as herds, food isn't exactly shared and the distribution is extremely selfish. In the case of lions for instance, the top-ranking individuals eat first, and will harshly chase off all others. Only when the alpha is sated, do the others get to eat, in order of social rank.
